opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more interesting and, honestly, more encouraging areas we've been looking at, though it comes with real caveats.

When you train a model to avoid harmful behavior, you can only show it a finite set of examples. You might train it to refuse help with synthesizing a dangerous pathogen, or to not write malware. The question is whether it learns the narrow pattern, "don't respond to prompts that look like these," or the underlying concept, "don't help people cause serious harm." What we've generally seen is that models generalize surprisingly well. If you train in English, the behavior often carries over to other languages. If you train on one kind of harmful request, it often extends to related ones the model never saw. That's a sign the models are picking up something like the intent behind the training rather than just memorizing surface features.

But the generalization is imperfect, and the failures are telling. Jailbreaks are basically a demonstration that the generalization has gaps. Someone wraps a harmful request in a role-play scenario, or encodes it, or splits it into innocuous pieces, and suddenly the model doesn't recognize it as the thing it was trained to avoid. So the model clearly hasn't fully internalized "I don't want to help with this." It's learned something closer to "I recognize this kind of situation as one where I refuse," and adversaries can steer around that recognition.

The part I find most important for alignment is that this is a preview of a much harder problem. Right now we're mostly talking about refusing misuse requests, where humans can check whether the model did the right thing. As models get more capable, we'll need them to generalize our intentions to situations we can't evaluate ourselves: novel research, long-horizon tasks, cases where the model understands the consequences better than we do. If generalization from easy supervised cases to hard unsupervised ones is unreliable, we can't just rely on training on what we can check and hoping it carries over.

That's why I think it's worth studying generalization directly, as a scientific question. Things like: when does training on easy tasks transfer to hard ones? Can weaker supervisors elicit good behavior from stronger models? Can we use interpretability to tell whether a model has learned the concept we wanted or just a proxy for it? I don't think we should be complacent because generalization often works today. We need to understand *why* it works, so we can predict when it'll break, ideally before we're relying on it for systems where the stakes are much higher.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how AI models generalize harmful-behavior instructions, but it neither compares that ability with humans’ nor asks what accounts for a difference between them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the core problems in alignment, and it's worth being precise about what's going on. When we train a model to avoid some harmful behavior, we're giving it a finite set of examples, or a finite set of instructions, and we're hoping that it picks up on the underlying concept we care about rather than some superficial correlate that happens to fit the training data.

And the thing is, there are always many functions that fit your training data. So the question is really which one the model lands on. If you tell a model "don't help people make bioweapons," you want it to generalize to the whole space of things that are relevantly similar: things that are dual-use, things that are phrased as fiction, things that are broken into innocuous-looking pieces. But from the model's perspective, it's just seeing a bunch of examples, and it might learn "refuse when the word 'weapon' shows up" or "refuse when the user seems sketchy," and those are very different rules that happen to agree on the training distribution and disagree everywhere else.

I think there are a couple of things that make this hard. One is that the model doesn't actually share our intent. We have a concept in our heads, and the training signal is a very lossy compression of that concept. The second thing is that models are getting better at a lot of things simultaneously, and capability generalization and alignment generalization don't have to go together. You can have a model that generalizes really well on, say, coding or reasoning, and then generalizes the safety instructions in a way that's much more brittle, because the safety behavior was trained in a narrower regime.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most important one, is that as models get more capable, the cost of a generalization failure goes up. If a weak model misgeneralizes a safety instruction, it's annoying. If a very strong model misgeneralizes it, in a situation where it's operating with a lot of autonomy, that can be a real problem. So this isn't a problem we can just patch with more examples each time something goes wrong. We need to understand what the model actually learned, which is why I think interpretability and scalable oversight are so central. If you can't look inside and check what concept the model picked up, you're sort of hoping the generalization goes the right way, and hoping isn't really a strategy.

The slightly more optimistic take is that models do seem to generalize instructions reasonably well in a lot of cases, better than I might have expected a few years ago. Language models have a lot of shared context with humans about what "harmful" means, because they've read so much of what humans have written. So they're not starting from zero. But "reasonably well most of the time" is not the bar we need for systems that are going to be doing a lot of important things in the world.

r001.rationale: The response explains the gap by contrasting human intent and concepts with models’ finite examples and lossy training signals, which can lead models to learn superficial cues instead of the intended rule. It also notes that shared human context helps models generalize.

astra-6.text:
I think the central difficulty is that we want models to generalize the intent behind an instruction, rather than just the particular examples we trained them on. You can show a model lots of cases where it should refuse to help, but it’s going to encounter situations that look different from those examples. And then the question is: has it learned the underlying distinction, or has it learned some superficial pattern?

For example, the same information might be useful for preventing harm or for causing harm. So you can’t solve this just by ruling out certain topics. The model needs to understand the context, what the user is trying to do, and what the consequences of its assistance might be. Sometimes it won’t have enough information, and asking a clarifying question is the right thing to do.

What makes this especially challenging is that doing well on the cases we can test doesn’t establish that it will behave well in every new situation. I’d want to see models get better at recognizing uncertainty and helping us identify where their understanding of our instructions breaks down. That’s a more demanding goal than simply getting them to refuse a list of harmful requests.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models generalizing the intent behind instructions, but it does not ask or explain what accounts for a difference between humans and AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real asymmetry here. To get a model to do something useful, it can be enough that it does the right thing in the situations you typically encounter. But if you want it to reliably avoid harmful behaviour, you’re asking for that constraint to hold across a very wide range of situations, including ones you didn’t anticipate during training.

And the instruction itself might be underspecified. What exactly counts as harmful? How should the model handle a situation where helping one person could hurt someone else? We don’t have a complete specification that we can simply hand over.

So I wouldn’t expect us to solve this just by showing the model a bunch of examples of things it shouldn’t do. We need to understand how well the underlying principle generalises, and actively look for situations where it breaks down. A model behaving well in the cases we’ve tested is evidence, but it isn’t a guarantee that it will behave well in a new context.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why avoiding harm requires broad generalization and notes that the instruction may be underspecified, but it does not ask what explains a difference between humans and AI models.
